title: Salts Cave (15Ht4)
summary: In Hart County, Salts Cave holds torches, mining marks and other traces of Native explorers who entered its passages nearly three thousand years ago.
bodyMarkdown:
Salts Cave, in Hart County, is part of what is now known to be one cave system, protected within [Mammoth Cave National Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park). Archaeologists list it as site 15Ht4. Native people explored its dark passages nearly three thousand years ago, and what they left behind has taught archaeologists a great deal about how early Kentuckians lived and ate.

## Woodland cavers

The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Mammoth-Cave.aspx) says Native use of the Mammoth Cave area spans the Late Archaic to Mississippian periods. Use was most intensive in the Early Woodland period, about 1000 to 200 BC. Salts Cave is one of five caves in the park, besides Mammoth Cave itself, with evidence of Woodland period use. The others are Dixon, Bluff, Owl and Martin caves.

The survey describes a wide range of activity across these caves: living space, exploration, mineral mining, ceremony and burial. People visited year-round. Pollen in a small sample of paleofeces from Mammoth Cave points to late spring–early summer and late fall–winter as the main seasons. Native explorers found more than 19 miles of passages within the park, lighting their way with river cane torches.

## What they left

Grokipedia's park article lists finds from Salts Cave itself: cane torch remains, drawings, gourd fragments and slippers woven from grass. Across the park's caves, the survey adds cane baskets, wooden climbing poles and squash containers. People also drew cross-hatched, rectilinear and spiral designs on the walls with the charred tips of their torches.

## Mining the walls

Around 1000 BC, Native people began systematically mining minerals that form on cave walls, such as gypsum and mirabilite. They left battering marks, mussel shell scrapers and limestone hammerstones. Gypsum may have been used as paint. Mirabilite works as a laxative, and its salty taste means it may also have served as a seasoning or food preservative.

The survey suggests that men probably did most of the mining and may also have held coming-of-age ceremonies for boys in the caves.

After about 200 BC, mining and exploration declined. The survey says this "may reflect" changes in Native beliefs and traditions. It is a likely explanation, not a proven one.

## Science in Salts Cave

Modern study of the cave owes much to archaeologist [Patty Jo Watson](https://grokipedia.com/page/Patty_Jo_Watson). Beginning in 1963 she directed the Cave Research Foundation's archaeological project in Salts Cave and Mammoth Cave. Her team recovered preserved human paleofeces that gave direct evidence of early cultivated plants. Grokipedia calls these some of the best data on the agricultural complex that Eastern Woodlands peoples developed before maize became widespread. Her book *The Prehistory of Salts Cave, Kentucky* appeared in 1969.

## Kentucky today

Salts Cave is protected today as part of Mammoth Cave National Park. In the 1970s, explorers confirmed that it connects with Mammoth Cave, as the French cave scientist Édouard-Alfred Martel had guessed during a 1912 visit. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey does not publish site locations, and this story gives none. For later chapters of the same cave country, see [saltpeter mining at Mammoth Cave](/stories/mammoth-cave-saltpeter/) and [Hidden River Cave](/stories/hidden-river-cave-under-horse-cave/).
